newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Iran crisis could depress world wheat market - AWB.
newsitem.headline: Iran crisis could depress world wheat market - AWB.

text.p: Political confrontation between Australia and Iran could depress world wheat prices if the standoff worsened, Australian wheat industry officials warned on Monday.

If the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) could not supply Iran with the two-to-three million tonnes of wheat it had contracted to sell in the 1996/97 year it would have to place the wheat on world markets, an AWB official told Reuters.
"We would expect the price would be lower than we get from Iran," the official said.

Uncertainty hung over Australia's A$500 million-A$600 million wheat trade with its main market, Iran, on Monday, despite Australian government assurances that any trade sanctions would not be retrospective.
Australian wheat farmers have urged the government to reject calls to ban trade with Iran after a German court fround Tehran ordered the mruders of four Kurdish activists in Berlin in 1992.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downers is reviewing relations with Iran after the court ruling and on Friday recalled ambassador Stuart Hume from Tehran.
Iran presently rates as Australia's biggest customer for wheat, having contracted to buy about 2.8 million tonnes of current-season grain.
Not all has been delivered and the AWB and the Australian government were waiting on Tehran's response to the Australian government's recall of its ambassador to Iran on Friday.
Iran regularly rates among Australia's largest wheat buyers. This year it is taking about 20 percent of Australia's wheat.
The AWB official told Reuters that political developments "do not affect the business commercially at this stage."
"We want to as usual talk to all of our clients about further sales," an AWB official said.
But officials with Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer told Reuters it was possible new sales and undelivered commodities could be affected.
The officials said it had been decided that Australian commodity exports to Iran would not be affected by trade sanctions which Australia might impose over the court finding.
But the Australian government and industry officials were still waiting on a reaction from Tehran over the recall of Australia's ambassador on Friday.
"That's why the ambassador has come back. It is possible (there could be future trade effects)," a Fischer official said.

Australian wheat forms the bulk of total Australian exports to Iran of A$650 million in calendar 1996. Other main items are coal, worth A$34.5 million, wool, worth A$12.3 million, and sugar, molasses and honey, worth A$11.3 million.
"As far as we're concerned, there's no problem. They're making a lot of noise but substantively there doesn't seem to have been a great deal of activity," Fischer's trade official said.
When asked when firm trade-related decisions might be made by either government, the official replied: "Got a crystal ball?"
